“Victoire” car mascot by René Lalique

René Lalique’s glass radiator mascot: a woman’s head whose hair streams back into a long fan of ribbed, clear glass, a symbol of speed.

Source
Victoria and Albert Museum: Victoire, CIRC.199-1972
Creator
René Lalique
Made
1928 (Musée Lalique); ca. 1925 (V&A)
Style
Art Deco (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Dynamic, glamorous, streamlined
Evidence

Open license, stored. License: CC-BY-SA-3.0. Rights policy

Context

The Musée Lalique dates Victoire to 1928 and says Lalique made it to mark the tenth anniversary of the 1918 armistice, for the bonnets of luxury cars. It notes that glass mascots were phased out in the 1930s and reissued as statuettes on a base. Musée Lalique.

The V&A records the object as a radiator mascot, manufacturer’s title “Victoire”, popular title “Spirit of the Wind”, press-moulded glass, 15.5 × 25 × 6.5 cm, made ca. 1925 (range 1920–1935), for the Lalique glassworks at Wingen-sur-Moder. V&A.

Observed

  • The head is in profile, with the mouth open and the eyes wide; the face and neck are frosted and smooth.
  • The hair sweeps back from the brow into a long, flat, rising fan of parallel ribs in clear glass that ends in a straight, slanted edge.
  • The ribs are close and regular and catch light as a series of bright lines.
  • The mascot sits on a short round frosted collar on a black display base.
  • Mold marks at the base are too faint in this photograph to read.

Why it belongs

The mascot turns speed into ornament: the wind is drawn as a regular fan of straight lines, the same radiating device the style uses for sunbursts.

It sits between core Art Deco and the later streamline branch: the subject is motion, but the form is still a stylized, symmetrical fan rather than a smooth teardrop.

Borrow

Draw motion as a fan of evenly spaced straight lines behind a simple shape.

Pair a matte surface with glossy parallel ridges for contrast in one material.
